title: Accessing Industry Research, Data, and Competitive Intelligence

questions.stem: The EFInA Access to Financial Services in Nigeria (A2F) survey is primarily used by insurance market researchers to:

opts.x: Verify the NIA's annual market share tables by providing alternative data on insurer performance.
Obtain demand-side data on insurance usage, awareness, barriers, and attitudes among Nigerian adults, which is unavailable from insurer or regulatory supply-side statistics.
Calculate the solvency margins of individual NAICOM-licensed insurers.
Provide actuarial mortality data for use in life insurance pricing.

questions.answer: (B) Obtain demand-side data on insurance usage, awareness, barriers, and attitudes among Nigerian adults, which is unavailable from insurer or regulatory supply-side statistics.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

The EFInA A2F survey is a nationally representative survey of Nigerian adults' access to and usage of financial services, including insurance. It is the primary source of demand-side data on the Nigerian insurance market: how many Nigerians have insurance; which types of insurance they hold; why they do not have insurance (awareness, affordability, trust); their attitudes toward insurance; and changes in these metrics over time. This demand-side perspective is entirely absent from insurer premium data (supply-side) and NAICOM regulatory statistics (supply-side), making the EFInA survey irreplaceable for understanding market penetration and the barriers to growth.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) The EFInA survey does not verify individual insurer performance, it provides population-level demand data.
(C) Solvency margins are calculated from insurer financial statements and NAICOM regulatory data, not consumer surveys.
(D) Actuarial mortality data is derived from life table analysis and insurer experience investigations, not from a general financial services usage survey.

questions.stem: Under the Freedom of Information Act 2011, a Nigerian insurance company requesting specific market data from NAICOM should expect the regulator to respond within:

opts.x: 24 hours for routine data requests.
7 days, with a possible extension of up to 21 additional days.
30 days in all circumstances.
90 days, reflecting the complexity of compiling regulatory data.

questions.answer: (B) 7 days, with a possible extension of up to 21 additional days.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

The Freedom of Information Act 2011 (FOIA) obliges public institutions to respond to information requests within 7 days of receipt. Where the institution requires additional time to compile information (for example, because the request involves complex data extraction from multiple sources), the Act permits an extension of up to 21 additional days, but the institution must notify the applicant of the extension and the reason within the initial 7-day window.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) 24 hours is not a standard FOIA response timeline, the Act prescribes 7 days as the standard.
(C) 30 days is the NDPA 2023 data subject access request response timeline, not the FOIA institutional response timeline.
(D) 90 days is far longer than the FOIA standard, using complexity as a general justification is inconsistent with the Act's intent to enable timely access to public information.

questions.stem: The Swiss Re Sigma publication series is best described as:

opts.x: A monthly newsletter published by the Swiss Federal Financial Market Supervisory Authority.
The insurance industry's most authoritative global research series, providing country-level market data, penetration statistics, and strategic analysis of global insurance trends.
A specialist publication on the Swiss domestic insurance market, published by the Swiss National Bank.
The quarterly journal of the Swiss Institute of Actuaries, covering life assurance reserving and pricing.

questions.answer: (B) The insurance industry's most authoritative global research series, providing country-level market data, penetration statistics, and strategic analysis of global insurance trends.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

Swiss Re Sigma is published by Swiss Re's Institute, the research arm of Swiss Re, one of the world's largest reinsurers. Sigma publications are produced annually (or on specific topics) and are the globally recognised benchmark for: insurance market size and penetration data by country; premium volume trends; catastrophe loss analysis; and thematic analysis of emerging insurance topics (InsurTech; ESG; climate risk; financial inclusion). For Nigerian insurance market researchers, Sigma provides the international benchmark data against which Nigeria's penetration can be compared.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Sigma is published by Swiss Re (a reinsurer), not by FINMA (the Swiss financial regulator).
(C) Sigma covers global insurance markets, not just the Swiss market.
(D) Sigma is a reinsurer research publication, not an actuarial professional body journal.

questions.stem: The NIA Annual Industry Statistics Report is valuable to the Nigerian insurance research function primarily because it:

opts.x: Provides real-time premium income data updated quarterly.
Publishes each licensed insurer's unaudited management accounts alongside the market aggregate data.
Consolidates market-level data on GWP, claims, and market share that enables benchmarking of the insurer's own performance against the market.
Contains NAICOM's annual enforcement actions and formal reprimands against individual insurers.

questions.answer: (C) Consolidates market-level data on GWP, claims, and market share that enables benchmarking of the insurer's own performance against the market.

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

The NIA's Annual Industry Statistics Report (published with a 6–12 month lag after year-end) consolidates NAICOM-submitted market data for all licensed insurers, providing: total industry GWP by class of business; total claims paid; market share by insurer; penetration data; and investment income trends. For an insurer's research function, this data enables: competitive benchmarking (is the insurer's market share growing or declining?); industry trend analysis (is the life market growing faster or slower than the insurer's own book?); and identification of market segments growing faster than the industry average.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) The NIA report is annual (or bi-annual), not real-time quarterly; there are significant data lags.
(B) Individual insurer management accounts are not publicly available in Nigeria, the NIA report provides market aggregate data, not individual insurer unaudited accounts.
(D) NAICOM enforcement actions are published separately, not in the NIA industry statistics report.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of a Competitive Intelligence (CI) function in a Nigerian life insurance company is:

opts.x: To conduct audits of competitor insurers on behalf of NAICOM.
To systematically gather, analyse, and distribute intelligence about the competitive, regulatory, and market environment to support the insurer's strategic decision-making.
To develop new insurance products by reverse-engineering competitors' product features.
To manage the insurer's own policyholder data analytics and CRM intelligence.

questions.answer: (B) To systematically gather, analyse, and distribute intelligence about the competitive, regulatory, and market environment to support the insurer's strategic decision-making.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

A Competitive Intelligence function is an internal capability that converts publicly available market, competitive, and regulatory information into actionable strategic intelligence. Its value is in: systematic monitoring (so important developments are not missed); analysis (converting raw information into strategic implications); and distribution (ensuring the right intelligence reaches the right decision-makers at the right time). CI functions monitor: competitor product launches and pricing; regulatory changes; market penetration data; consumer attitude surveys; and emerging technology developments.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Conducting audits of competitor insurers is a regulatory function: CI functions gather publicly available intelligence, not conduct inspections with regulatory authority.
(C) Reverse-engineering competitor products may be part of the competitive analysis, but it is a narrow sub-activity, not the primary purpose of a CI function.
(D) Managing the insurer's own policyholder data analytics is a CRM/data analytics function, distinct from competitive intelligence, which focuses on external market information.

questions.stem:
A Nigerian life insurer’s strategy team is preparing a market entry assessment for a proposed expansion into Group Family Takaful for northern Nigerian state government employers.
(a) Identify and describe five specific Nigerian and international data sources the research team should access to size the target market and understand the competitive landscape.
(b) Describe the top-down market sizing methodology the team should use, identifying the specific data inputs required at each stage.
(c) Explain how the EFInA A2F survey data and PenCom data would each contribute to the market sizing exercise.
(d) Describe one FOI request the insurer could submit to obtain regulatory data not routinely published, and explain what intelligence it would provide.

model.h: Part (a): Five Data Sources

rows: Data Source
Relevance to Market Sizing and Competitive Landscape
1. PenCom Annual Report and CPS Statistics

Northern Nigeria state government employee CPS participation data. Provides: total formal sector employees by state; RSA balance distribution; employer registration status. Directly sizes the 'employer with formal sector workforce' target market.
2. National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) State Statistical Bulletins

State-level data on employment by sector; formal vs informal sector split; government employment as a proportion of total formal employment. Provides the macro-demographic foundation for the market size calculation.
3. EFInA Access to Financial Services Survey

Demand-side data: insurance penetration among adults in northern Nigeria; awareness of Takaful products specifically; barriers to adoption; attitudes toward conventional vs Islamic financial products. Critical for understanding consumer readiness and the marketing challenge.
4. NAICOM Takaful Operational Guidelines and licensed Takaful operators list

Regulatory framework and competitive landscape: which Takaful operators are currently licensed; what products have received NAICOM approval; what are the Takaful-specific capital and governance requirements for a new entrant. Determines the regulatory feasibility of market entry.
5. Swiss Re Sigma African Insurance Market Reports; African Development Bank economic data

International benchmarking of Takaful penetration in comparable Muslim-majority markets (Egypt, Kenya, Malaysia); premium rates; product structures. Provides the market development trajectory to inform projections for Nigerian Takaful market growth.

model.h: Part (b): Top-Down Market Sizing Methodology

Stage 1: Total Addressable Market (TAM):
Data input: NBS total employment in northern Nigerian states (Kano, Kaduna, Katsina, Sokoto, Niger, Jigawa, Kebbi, Zamfara, Gombe, Borno, Adamawa, Yobe, Bauchi, Taraba, Nasarawa, Plateau, Benue).
Calculation: Total formal sector employment in northern Nigeria × average annual emoluments × 3 (PRA 2014 minimum group life benefit) = total insurance sum assured addressable. Multiply by the group life premium rate (0.15% of sum assured) to get the TAM in annual premium income.

Stage 2: Serviceable Addressable Market (SAM):
Data input: Proportion of formal sector employment that is state government employment (NBS data); employers that do not already hold group life insurance (estimated gap from PenCom compliance data).
Calculation: TAM × (state government employer share) × (% non-compliant with PRA 2014) = SAM; the share of the TAM that is specifically addressable by a state government Takaful scheme.

Stage 3: Serviceable Obtainable Market (SOM):
Data input: Current Takaful operator competitive landscape; estimated market share the insurer can realistically win in 3 years.
Calculation: SAM × realistic market share target (e.g., 30% in year 3 given first-mover advantage in state government partnerships) = SOM, the insurer's realistic revenue opportunity.

Year 1–3 premium income projection: SOM × assumed phase-in rate (Year 1: 30% of SAM target; Year 2: 65%; Year 3: 100%).
Part (c): Contribution of EFInA A2F and PenCom Data

EFInA A2F contribution:
The EFInA A2F survey provides the demand-side foundation for the market sizing: what proportion of northern Nigerian adults currently have any insurance; whether they are aware of Takaful as an alternative to conventional insurance; what specific barriers prevent them from taking out insurance (affordability, awareness, trust, religious concerns about conventional insurance); and whether they express preference for Takaful products. This data:
• Validates the existence of the opportunity (if northern Nigerians express preference for Takaful but conventional insurance penetration is very low, the addressable market is large).
• Informs the marketing strategy (if the primary barrier is awareness, marketing investment should precede product launch; if the barrier is affordability, product pricing must be the first investment).

PenCom data contribution:
PenCom's annual report shows: the number of registered CPS contributors by state; the employer registration status by state (which employers are registered with a PFA and therefore have formal sector workforces); and RSA balance distribution. This data:
• Provides the most reliable count of formal sector employers in each northern state.
• Identifies which state government employers are PRA 2014 registered and therefore legally obligated to maintain group life insurance.
• Identifies the subset of employers that are registered but for whom there is no record of a group life insurance policy (through cross-referencing PenCom employer registration with NAICOM group life policy data), the directly addressable non-compliant market.
Part (d): FOI Request and Intelligence It Would Provide

FOI request to NAICOM:
'Please provide data on the number and total sum assured of group life insurance policies currently in force for employers in each of the following northern Nigerian states [list 12 states], broken down by: (a) private sector employers; and (b) state government and public sector employers. If this data is not maintained by NAICOM in this format, please advise what group life data is available by state or sector.'

Intelligence this would provide:
1. Existing market penetration among state government employers: If NAICOM data shows that 45% of northern state government employers already hold group life insurance, the non-compliant market (the target) is the remaining 55%.
2. Competitive concentration: If 3 insurers hold 80% of northern state government group life policies, the competitive landscape is concentrated and entry requires a differentiated value proposition (Takaful product design; better service; lower premium) to displace incumbents.
3. Size validation: Comparing NAICOM group life sum assured data against the NBS employment data and PRA 2014 minimum calculation reveals the coverage adequacy gap, how many employers are nominally compliant but are providing below-PRA 2014 minimum benefits.

questions.stem:
A mid-size Nigerian life insurer with 250 employees wants to build its first dedicated competitive intelligence function. The MD/CEO has approved a budget of ₦45 million per year for the function.
(a) Design the team structure for this CI function, specifying the roles, responsibilities, and required profiles.
(b) Design an annual research calendar for the function, identifying the key data source monitoring activities by quarter.
(c) Describe the five standard report templates the function should produce and their respective distribution frameworks.
(d) Explain how the CI function should measure and communicate its impact to justify its budget at the annual ExCo review.

model.h: Part (a): Team Structure

rows: Role
Responsibilities and Profile
Head of CI / Market Research (Senior Manager)

Owns the annual research agenda; presents findings to senior management and the Board; manages external research partnerships; responsible for budget. Profile: 5–8 years' research or strategy consulting experience; insurance sector knowledge; strong analytical and communication skills. Salary: ₦18–₦22m per annum.
Quantitative Research Analyst

Designs and analyses large-scale quantitative surveys; manages data from EFInA, NBS, NAICOM, and NIA; builds market sizing models; produces data visualisations. Profile: 3–5 years' quantitative research experience; strong Excel/R/Python skills; insurance or financial services data experience preferred. Salary: ₦9–₦12m.
Competitive Intelligence Analyst

Monitors competitor activity (product launches, pricing, NAICOM filings, news); conducts mystery shopping programmes; prepares competitor analysis reports. Profile: 2–4 years' market research or insurance experience; systematic researcher; excellent written communication. Salary: ₦7–₦10m.
Research Operations Coordinator

Manages external agency relationships; coordinates field research logistics; maintains the research data library; administers the function's reporting calendar. Profile: 1–3 years' research operations or project management experience. Salary: ₦4–₦6m.

model.h: External research budget (₦45m total, minus ₦38–₦50m salary budget leaves ₦0–₦7m for external): The budget is very tight for a full team plus external research. Recommendation: reduce the team to 3 FTEs (Head, one Analyst covering both quantitative and CI, and one Coordinator) at ₦25–₦30m total salary, allocating ₦15–₦20m to external research agency commissioning.
Part (b): Annual Research Calendar

rows: Quarter
Key Data Source Monitoring and Research Activities
Q1 (Jan–Mar)

NIA Annual Industry Statistics Report analysis (prior year data typically released Q1); NAICOM annual regulatory return analysis; EFInA A2F report review (if new edition); Annual competitor product portfolio review (review all NAICOM product approvals issued in prior year); Strategic plan assumption refresh based on Q4 prior-year data.
Q2 (Apr–Jun)

Primary research fieldwork: consumer trust and insurance perception survey (biennial); Mystery shopping programme (competitor selling practices); NBS quarterly economic data review; Swiss Re Sigma annual World Insurance Report analysis; Mid-year market share estimation using available partial-year NAICOM data.
Q3 (Jul–Sep)

NAICOM regulatory developments monitoring (new guidelines, consultation papers, draft regulations); Competitor product launch monitoring; PenCom quarterly data review; Lapsed customer research, qualitative exit interviews with policyholders who lapsed in the past 12 months.
Q4 (Oct–Dec)

Annual strategic planning support: preparation of the market intelligence input to the insurer's annual strategy review; Competitive benchmarking report for the Board; Annual research calendar planning for the following year; EFInA, NIA, and NAICOM FOI requests for any data not publicly available.

model.h: Part (c): Five Standard Report Templates

rows: Report
Frequency and Distribution
Monthly Competitive Monitor

Monthly; 2–3 pages. Key developments: competitor product launches; NAICOM regulatory actions; significant market news; pricing changes detected through mystery shopping. Distribution: MD/CEO; CDO; Chief Technical Officer. Turnaround: 5th of each month.
Quarterly Market Dashboard

Quarterly; 8–10 pages. Market-level metrics: industry GWP growth; market share trend; penetration data; NPS benchmarking; key regulatory updates. Distribution: ExCo; Board Risk Committee. Turnaround: within 15 days of quarter-end.
Annual Competitive Landscape Report

Annual; 20–30 pages. Comprehensive competitor analysis: product benchmarking across all major product lines; distribution model analysis; digital capability assessment; market share trends. Distribution: ExCo; Board (as part of strategic plan input). Timing: September/October (for use in Q4 strategy planning).
Biennial Consumer Research Report

Every two years; 25–40 pages. Primary research findings from the consumer trust, awareness, and insurance adoption survey. Distribution: ExCo; Board; product development team; marketing team. Timing: aligned with EFInA A2F publication cycle.
Ad Hoc Market Entry / Product Intelligence Report

As needed; 10–20 pages. Deep-dive on a specific market opportunity or product category (e.g., the Takaful market sizing exercise in Q6). Distribution: Strategy team; relevant functional head; MD/CEO. Timing: within 6 weeks of commissioning.

model.h: Part (d): Measuring and Communicating CI Function Impact

The CI function should measure its impact through three mechanisms:

1. Decision attribution: Maintain a log of significant strategic or product decisions made in the year, noting whether CI research materially informed the decision. At the annual ExCo review, present a 'decision impact summary' (for example: 'Our Q2 consumer research revealed that trust, not affordability, is the primary barrier in the 25–35 demographic) which led to the decision to invest ₦30m in claims storytelling content marketing rather than premium discounting. This decision, informed by research, avoided spending ₦30m on an approach the data suggested would not work.'

2. Competitive advantage evidence: Show cases where the CI function identified a market opportunity before a competitor moved on it, or identified a competitor initiative in time to prepare a response. 'In March, our competitive monitor identified that Insurer X was preparing to launch a digital group life product for SMEs. We accelerated our own product development timeline and launched two weeks before them, securing three corporate accounts that might have gone to the competitor.'

3. Research consumption metrics: Track how many times research outputs are cited in strategy documents, product proposals, and Board papers, demonstrating that research is being used in decisions, not sitting in a library. A quarterly 'research usage report' showing which publications were referenced in which decisions is a simple but powerful demonstration of value.

questions.stem:
A Nigerian life insurer’s strategy team has produced a competitive intelligence report citing the following sources:
(i) A 2019 EFInA survey claiming that only 3% of Nigerians have life insurance;
(ii) A 2024 social media post from an insurance consultant claiming that the Nigerian group life market is worth ₦800 billion;
(iii) A 2024 Munich Re African Insurance Market report estimating Nigerian life insurance GWP at a defined level; (iv) A 2025 NAICOM press release stating the industry’s GWP for Q1 2025.
(a) For each source, evaluate its reliability using the quality assessment criteria in this chapter, noting any specific concerns.
(b) Rank the four sources in order of research quality and explain your ranking.
(c) Describe what additional data the team should seek to supplement or validate each source.
(d) Explain the strategic risk of relying on the weakest-quality sources in the report when presenting to the Board.

model.h: Part (a): Source Reliability Evaluation

rows: Source
Reliability Assessment
(i) 2019 EFInA Survey, 3% life insurance penetration

CONCERNS: Six years old as of 2025. Given that NIIRA 2025 was implemented in 2025 and the credit life mandate has been partially operationalised since 2022, insurance penetration data from 2019 may significantly understate the current position. The EFInA A2F survey is methodologically rigorous and nationally representative (STRENGTH), but the age of the data is a serious reliability concern for current market sizing. Use as directional historical benchmark only; seek the most recent EFInA edition.
(ii) 2024 social media post from an insurance consultant, group life market ₦800bn

MAJOR CONCERNS: Source is unverified; a social media post from an unnamed consultant has no methodological rigour, no peer review, and no audit trail. The ₦800bn figure cannot be validated without knowing the methodology. Social media posts can be estimates, opinions, extrapolations from partial data, or simply invented. This source should not be used in a Board-level report without independent corroboration from a primary source (NAICOM statistics; NIA Annual Report).
(iii) 2024 Munich Re African Insurance Market Report: Nigerian life GWP

HIGH RELIABILITY: Munich Re is a major global reinsurer with substantial operations in Africa. Its African Insurance Market reports are based on a combination of: reinsurer cedant data (Munich Re sees a significant portion of Nigerian insurance premiums through its treaty relationships); publicly available regulatory statistics; and proprietary analysis. The 2024 publication date makes this current. Limitations: Munich Re's data may reflect primarily the formal, reinsured segment, microinsurance and USSD-distributed products may be underrepresented.
(iv) 2025 NAICOM press release: Q1 2025 GWP

HIGHEST RELIABILITY for the specific figure: NAICOM is the regulatory authority; its quarterly GWP statistics are based on mandatory insurer returns. The Q1 2025 data is current. Limitations: press release data may be preliminary (not yet fully audited); Q1 figures are seasonal (not directly annualisable without seasonal adjustment). However, for the specific question of current market size, this is the most authoritative source available.

model.h: Part (b): Ranking in Order of Research Quality

Rank 1 (highest quality): Source (iv), 2025 NAICOM press release. Primary regulatory data; most current; authoritative source for the Nigerian market.

Rank 2: Source (iii), 2024 Munich Re African Insurance Market Report. Credible, methodologically rigorous, recent; based on primary industry data. Slight limitation: partial market coverage.

Rank 3: Source (i), 2019 EFInA Survey. Methodologically rigorous and nationally representative, but the 6-year age of the data significantly reduces its current reliability.

Rank 4 (lowest quality): Source (ii), 2024 social media post. No methodology; no verification; no peer review; cannot be cited in a professional Board-level document without independent corroboration.
Part (c): Additional Data to Supplement or Validate Each Source

Source (i), 2019 EFInA Survey: The team should obtain the most recent EFInA A2F survey edition (2024 if available; 2022 if 2024 is not yet published), and submit a FOI request to EFInA for any interim data published since the last full survey.

Source (ii): Social media post: The ₦800bn group life market figure should be validated against: NIA Annual Industry Statistics (which publishes GWP by class of business, including group life separately); NAICOM's quarterly return aggregate data; and the Munich Re report's Nigeria breakdown. If none of these sources supports the ₦800bn figure, it should be excluded from the Board report.

Source (iii): Munich Re report: Cross-reference against the NAICOM Q1 2025 data (Source iv) to validate the order of magnitude. If Munich Re's 2024 annual estimate is consistent with the implied annual run rate from NAICOM's Q1 2025 figure, the Munich Re data is corroborated.

Source (iv): NAICOM press release: Follow up with NAICOM's quarterly statistical report (more detailed than a press release); cross-reference against NIA Annual Statistics for the most recent full year; annualise Q1 data with appropriate seasonal adjustment (life insurance GWP tends to be higher in Q1 due to group life scheme renewals in January).
Part (d): Strategic Risk of Relying on Weakest-Quality Sources

Presenting a strategic recommendation to the Board based on the social media consultant's ₦800bn market size figure, without corroboration from primary sources, creates three specific strategic risks:

1. Decision quality risk: If the market is actually ₦350bn (not ₦800bn), an investment decision calibrated to a ₦800bn opportunity will significantly over-invest in entry costs, distribution infrastructure, and premium capacity, expecting returns that cannot materialise at the actual market size.

2. Board credibility risk: If a Board member independently researches the group life market and cannot find corroboration for the ₦800bn figure (or worse, finds NIA statistics that suggest a different number) the strategy team's credibility is destroyed. A single uncorroborated source that a Board member disproves invalidates the entire presentation in the Board's perception.

3. Regulatory risk: If the strategy is subsequently questioned by NAICOM (in the context of a product approval or a market entry filing), and the market sizing is based on a social media post, the insurer's regulatory due diligence will appear inadequate.

Conclusion: The social media post (Source ii) should be explicitly excluded from the Board presentation. The correct approach is to note in the research methodology: 'A market estimate of ₦800bn was cited in a 2024 market commentary but could not be validated from primary sources; this figure has therefore been excluded from the market sizing analysis.' This honest acknowledgement of a source quality limitation is far more professionally credible than presenting an unverified figure as if it were authoritative research.

questions.stem: The Nigerian insurance industry’s strategic decision-making is widely observed to be based more on convention, competitor imitation, and management intuition than on systematic market research and competitive intelligence. Critically evaluate why this is the case, and assess what the industry would need to change (in terms of research infrastructure, management culture, regulatory transparency, and data availability) to become genuinely research-driven. In your answer, discuss: the specific gaps in the Nigerian insurance data environment that make evidence-based strategy harder than in more developed markets; the internal organisational barriers to building effective CI functions in Nigerian insurers; the role that NAICOM, the NIA, and EFInA could play in improving the data environment; and the commercial case for the individual insurer that invests in building research-driven decision-making ahead of its peers.

model.h: Thesis

The observation is accurate and consequential. An industry that makes strategic decisions based on competitor imitation will always be a market follower, systematically reacting to market changes rather than anticipating or creating them. For a market with Nigeria's penetration potential, the opportunity cost of intuition-driven strategy is enormous. But the roots of the problem are structural, not merely cultural, and addressing them requires systemic change across four dimensions simultaneously.
Why Nigerian Insurance Strategic Decision-Making Is Convention-Driven

1. Absence of research infrastructure: Most Nigerian life insurers do not have a dedicated market research function. Without a research function, strategic decisions default to the available information, which is typically: (a) the MD/CEO's subjective interpretation of market conversations; (b) competitor actions that are publicly visible (a competitor launches a new product, so 'we must launch something similar'); and (c) internal financial data that describes historical performance but provides no insight into future market dynamics.

2. Data environment limitations: The Nigerian insurance data environment is significantly less rich than comparable financial services markets:
• NAICOM publishes aggregate market data with significant time lags (often 12–18 months).
• Individual insurer data is not publicly comparable; there is no equivalent of the UK's FCA sector data or South Africa's FSB market reports that enable granular competitive benchmarking.
• Demand-side data (EFInA A2F) is available only biennially and is not insurance-sector-specific enough for the product-level decisions insurers need to make.

3. Management culture undervaluing evidence: Where markets are relatively undifferentiated (similar products, similar distribution, similar pricing across all players), the returns to research investment are low, because the insurer that discovers a market insight cannot easily protect the first-mover advantage before competitors imitate. This creates a collective action problem: no insurer invests heavily in research because the insights will be quickly replicated by competitors.

4. Cost vs perceived value: Research is expensive relative to the perceived immediate return, a ₦45m research function budget versus the zero apparent cost of 'management intuition' creates a budget allocation bias against research in organisations with short-term performance pressure.
What Must Change: Research Infrastructure

The minimum investment for a research-driven Nigerian life insurer is:
• A dedicated CI function (as described in Q7), with qualified staff, a systematic monitoring programme, and a mandate to produce actionable intelligence rather than descriptive reports.
• A primary research programme, at minimum a biennial consumer survey and an annual competitor product review.
• Integration of the research function with product development and strategy, through the governance mechanisms described in Q8 (Gate 1 research evidence requirement; annual strategy research review).

The NIA should consider facilitating industry-shared research infrastructure, a sector-wide consumer survey (jointly funded by all NIA members) that provides more frequent and more specific demand-side data than the EFInA A2F survey alone.
Management Culture Change

The management culture change required is from 'HiPPO decision-making' (Highest Paid Person's Opinion) to evidence-based decision-making:
• Senior leaders must visibly base decisions on research rather than on intuition, citing evidence in ExCo and Board presentations rather than personal conviction.
• Product development gate requirements (Gate 1 consumer insight evidence) must be enforced, and not waived because 'the CEO has a strong feeling about this product.'
• Research findings that contradict the CEO's prior view must be able to be presented without social or political consequence, requiring a psychologically safe research culture at the senior level.

This cultural change is driven most effectively by the CEO modelling research-driven decision-making, asking 'what does the evidence show?' before 'what do I think?' in every strategic discussion.
Regulatory Transparency and Data Availability

NAICOM can significantly improve the insurance data environment with relatively modest investment:

1. Quarterly GWP publication by product class: More frequent, more granular market data would enable insurers to detect market trend shifts within quarters rather than retrospectively.

2. Individual insurer performance publication: Publishing each licensed insurer's key performance metrics (GWP growth; claims ratio; market share; NPS if collected), with appropriate insurer consent, would enable genuine competitive benchmarking and create performance transparency that incentivises improvement.

3. Standardised product disclosure data: If all NAICOM product approval applications included standardised premium rate data, the market would have a shared pricing benchmark that enables competitive intelligence without requiring individual insurer espionage.

4. NAICOM research programme: NAICOM should commission (with industry funding) an annual Nigerian Insurance Market Research Report (modelled on the South African Financial Sector Conduct Authority's sector studies) providing a comprehensive evidence base for industry strategy and regulatory policy simultaneously.
The Commercial Case for the First Mover

Despite the collective action problem, the individual insurer that invests in research infrastructure ahead of its peers captures a genuine first-mover advantage:

1. Earlier identification of growth opportunities (Group Family Takaful in northern Nigeria; USSD microinsurance for informal sector traders), before competitors recognise them.

2. Superior product-market fit, products designed from consumer insight rather than from competitor imitation are more likely to meet genuine customer needs, generating better persistency and lower lapse rates.

3. Talent attraction, the most analytically capable professionals want to work in organisations where evidence matters and where their research skills are valued. The insurer with a genuine research function is more attractive to the talent pool it most needs to build the analytical capabilities required for AI, data-driven underwriting, and precision marketing.

questions.stem: ‘In the Nigerian insurance market, the most powerful competitive intelligence tool is not Bloomberg, Swiss Re Sigma, or the NIA market share tables. It is a systematic, continuous programme of listening to Nigerian insurance consumers (their needs, their fears, their objections, their experiences) and translating that listening into product, distribution, and service decisions that are genuinely responsive to what people actually want. The insurers that commit to this consumer listening programme, and to the organisational discipline required to act on what they hear, will build businesses that are structurally more competitive than those that rely on competitor monitoring and market data alone.’ Critically evaluate this proposition and design a comprehensive consumer research programme for a Nigerian life insurer, addressing: research design, sample composition, question areas, frequency, institutional partnerships, and the governance mechanisms for translating consumer insight into management action.

model.h: Thesis

The proposition is substantially correct, and represents a genuinely radical reorientation for an industry that has historically been supply-driven (we offer these products through these channels) rather than demand-driven (we design products and channels around what consumers actually want and fear). But the proposition should not be read as rejecting the value of market statistics and competitive data; it is arguing for the primacy of consumer insight as the foundation on which all other market intelligence is built.
Why Consumer Listening Is the Most Powerful CI Tool

All other competitive intelligence sources (NIA market share tables; Swiss Re Sigma; NAICOM regulatory data) describe what has happened, historical market performance. Consumer listening describes what will happen; the latent demand and unmet needs that will define the market's future. The insurer who knows that 73% of Lagos market traders would pay ₦500/week for a product that clearly pays their family on death, but that only 12% believe any insurance company would actually pay, has a competitive insight that is not available in any published data source.

Additionally, consumer listening creates a self-reinforcing feedback loop that gradually separates the insurer from its competitors: products designed from consumer insight generate better customer satisfaction; better customer satisfaction generates higher NPS; higher NPS generates more referrals; more referrals generate more policyholders without additional acquisition cost.
Comprehensive Consumer Research Programme Design

Programme architecture: four complementary research streams running continuously throughout the year.

Stream 1: Quantitative brand and attitude tracking (biennial, N=3,000 nationally representative):
Research question: What is the current state of insurance awareness, trust, adoption, and price sensitivity across Nigerian adult demographics?
Sample composition: Nationally representative by region (South-West, South-East, South-South, North-Central, North-West, North-East); by urbanisation (urban, peri-urban, rural); by income proxy (formal employment, informal sector, self-employment); and by gender (50/50).
Question areas: Spontaneous and aided awareness of insurance; current insurance holdings; primary barriers to insurance adoption; experience with insurance claims; trust drivers and destroyers; product preference and willingness to pay; preferred communication channels and languages.
Frequency: Every two years (aligned with EFInA A2F publication cycle to enable benchmarking).
Institutional partnership: Commission through a nationally accredited market research firm (NOI Polls; Kantar Nigeria) to ensure methodological rigour and fieldwork quality.

Stream 2: Continuous policyholder satisfaction tracking (monthly, N=150 per month):
Research question: How do our current policyholders experience our products, service, and claims handling?
Sample: Random selection of 150 policyholders who had a policy interaction (claim; premium payment; service call; policy anniversary) in the previous month.
Question areas: Post-interaction CSAT; NPS score; specific feedback on the interaction quality; likelihood to renew; likelihood to recommend.
Frequency: Monthly, providing 1,800 interviews per year with a cumulative quarterly dataset of 450 interviews.
Governance: Monthly report to ExCo; quarterly trend report to the Board Audit Committee.

Stream 3: Lapsed and surrendered policyholder exit research (quarterly, N=40–50 per quarter):
Research question: Why do policyholders leave us? What would have retained them?
Sample: Policyholders who lapsed or surrendered in the previous quarter, contacted with specific consent for the exit interview.
Method: 30-minute telephone interviews with structured questionnaire and open-ended sections for narrative feedback.
Insights feed: Directly into the product development and conservation programme redesign.

Stream 4: Prospective consumer qualitative research (biennial, N=8–12 focus groups):
Research question: What do non-policyholders actually want from insurance? What would make them buy?
Sample: Participants who do not currently hold insurance and are in the insurer's target segments (informal sector traders; young urban professionals; rural Ajo group members).
Method: 2-hour focus group discussions with a trained moderator, conducted in the participant's language (Yoruba, Hausa, Igbo, Pidgin as appropriate).
Insights feed: Product design gate reviews; marketing message development; distribution model decisions.
Governance Mechanisms for Translating Insight into Management Action

1. Research-to-decision log: Every research report is accompanied by a 'So What?' section, three to five specific management actions recommended based on the findings. Each action is assigned to a named accountable owner with a defined timeline. The research log tracks whether each recommended action was implemented or explicitly rejected (with documented rationale).

2. Quarterly consumer insight review: A quarterly 60-minute ExCo session dedicated exclusively to consumer research findings, requiring the Head of CI to present the quarter's key insights; the product, distribution, and service heads to respond with what actions they are taking; and the CEO to hold them accountable for actions committed in the previous quarter.

3. Board-level consumer dashboard: The Board receives a quarterly consumer dashboard covering: NPS trend; CSAT trend; top three consumer-cited barriers to insurance adoption; top three sources of policyholder dissatisfaction. This ensures Board-level visibility of the consumer reality, not filtered through management's optimism.

4. Product development gate 1 standard: The six-gate product innovation process requires consumer insight evidence at Gate 1. No new product proceeds to actuarial pricing or regulatory filing without documented evidence, from either primary research or secondary consumer data, that the proposed product addresses a genuine, sized consumer need.
Budget and ROI Justification

A comprehensive four-stream consumer research programme for a mid-size Nigerian life insurer costs approximately ₦25–₦35m per year, covering field research costs, data analysis, and reporting. The commercial ROI justification:

1. Product-market fit: Products designed from consumer insight have higher adoption rates and lower lapse rates. A 5-point persistency improvement (from 65% to 70% 13-month persistency) on a ₦50bn in-force book generates approximately ₦2.5bn additional annual renewal premium, a 100× return on the research investment.

2. Marketing effectiveness: Consumer insight enables more targeted marketing messages, reducing the cost of acquiring each new customer by concentrating spend on messages and channels that the research has confirmed resonate with the target demographic.

3. Strategic de-risking: A ₦500m investment in a new digital distribution channel that is validated by consumer research before launch is more likely to succeed than one based purely on competitor imitation. The research investment is insurance on the strategic investment.
